items.definition: Connected with the economy, trade and money in a country. Do not confuse it with economical, which means cheap to use or not wasteful.
examples: The government has announced a new economic plan.
Rising prices are causing economic problems for many families.

items.definition: Using little money, fuel or time; good value. It describes things or people who do not waste resources, not the economy of a country (that is economic).
examples: A small hybrid car is more economical than a big saloon.
It is more economical to buy vegetables in bulk.
collocations: an economical way of doing something

items.definition: To have an influence on someone or something; to change it. It is usually a verb, while effect is usually a noun.
examples: The strike will affect thousands of commuters.
Poor sleep affects my concentration.

items.definition: A change that is the result of something. Use effect as a noun (the effect of noise on sleep); the verb that means to influence is affect.
examples: The new law had a positive effect on small businesses.
The medicine began to take effect after twenty minutes.

items.definition: To lift something or to increase it; it always has an object (raise prices). Compare rise, which has no object and happens by itself.
examples: The council plans to raise parking charges next year.
Please raise your hand if you have a question.

items.definition: To go up or increase by itself, with no object (prices rise). Its forms are rise, rose, risen; compare raise, which needs someone or something to do the lifting.
examples: House prices have risen sharply over the last decade.
The sun rises later in winter.

items.definition: To take money or property from a person or place, often using force. The object is the victim or place (rob a bank); what you take is stolen.
examples: Two men robbed a post office in the town centre.
He was robbed of his wallet on the underground.

items.definition: To take something that belongs to someone else without permission. The object is the thing taken (steal a bike); the person or place is robbed.
examples: Someone stole my bicycle from outside the library.
She had her phone stolen on the bus.

items.definition: To give something to someone for a short time, expecting to get it back. The owner lends; the other person borrows.
examples: Could you lend me your charger until tomorrow?
The bank agreed to lend them money for the flat.

items.definition: To take something from someone for a short time, with their permission, and give it back later. You borrow from someone; they lend to you.
examples: Can I borrow your umbrella? I'll bring it back on Monday.
They had to borrow money from the bank to start the business.

items.definition: Important enough to be remembered in history, or famous because of its past. It is not the same as historical, which only means connected with history.
examples: The two leaders signed a historic agreement.
We spent the morning in the historic centre of York.

items.definition: Connected with the study of the past or with something that really happened in the past. It does not suggest importance; for that, use historic.
examples: She writes historical novels set in the nineteenth century.
There is little historical evidence for the story.

items.definition: To suggest something without saying it directly. The speaker or writer implies; the listener or reader infers.
examples: Are you implying that I made a mistake?
His silence seemed to imply that he disagreed.

items.definition: To reach a conclusion from the evidence or hints you have, even if nobody said it directly. The listener or reader infers; the speaker or writer implies.
examples: From her tone, I inferred that she was not happy.
We can infer from the figures that sales are falling.
